question: What does incrementing the MAJOR version in Semantic Versioning indicate?

options.text: The project transitioned from alpha to stable
options.explanation: Transitioning from alpha/beta to stable is a specific point in history, not the rule for MAJOR. MAJOR is determined by the presence of breaking changes.

options.text: New functionality was added that is backward compatible with the previous version
options.explanation: This describes a MINOR version. New features without breaking the existing API only bump MINOR.

options.text: Changes were introduced that are incompatible with the previous API (breaking changes)
options.explanation: Correct. MAJOR is incremented only for breaking changes — when existing users' code stops working without modifications on their part.

options.text: Bugs were fixed without changing the public API
options.explanation: This describes a PATCH version. Fixing a bug without changing the interface only bumps PATCH.

question: In GitLab CI you want to run a release job only when tags like v1.2.3, v2.0.0, v10.5.2 appear. Which rule should you use?

options.text: only: [tags]
options.explanation: only: [tags] will run the job for ANY tag, including dev-tag, hotfix-test, my-tag. For filtering by semver format, a regex is needed.
only: [/^v.*/] will match any tag starting with v, including v-test, v-broken, v, or vXXX. This is too broad.

options.text: rules: - if: '$CI_COMMIT_TAG =~ /^v\d+\.\d+\.\d+$/'
options.explanation: Correct. The regex /^v\d+\.\d+\.\d+$/ precisely matches the vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH format. Only tags in this format will trigger the job.

options.text: rules: - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'
options.explanation: This will run the job on every commit to main, but not on tags. CI_COMMIT_BRANCH and CI_COMMIT_TAG are different variables.

question: Which GitLab CI variable contains the tag name that triggered the pipeline?

options.text: GIT_TAG
options.explanation: GIT_TAG is not a standard GitLab CI variable. It does not exist in the list of predefined variables.

options.text: CI_RELEASE_VERSION
options.explanation: CI_RELEASE_VERSION is not a standard GitLab CI variable. This is a nonexistent name.

options.text: CI_COMMIT_TAG
options.explanation: Correct. CI_COMMIT_TAG is a predefined GitLab variable. It contains the tag name (e.g., v1.2.3) and is only available in pipelines triggered by a tag.

options.text: CI_TAG_NAME
options.explanation: This variable does not exist in GitLab CI. You need to know the exact name of predefined variables.

question: A git tag has the value v1.2.3. How do you correctly strip the 'v' prefix when publishing an npm package?

options.text: export VERSION=$(semver $CI_COMMIT_TAG)
options.explanation: semver is a separate tool not installed by default. For simply removing 'v', this is overkill.

options.text: npm version $CI_COMMIT_TAG — npm will strip 'v' automatically
options.explanation: npm does not strip 'v' automatically. npm version v1.2.3 will return an error because v1.2.3 is not a valid semver string for npm.

options.text: export VERSION=${CI_COMMIT_TAG#v}
options.explanation: Correct. Bash parameter expansion ${var#prefix} removes the prefix. ${CI_COMMIT_TAG#v} turns v1.2.3 into 1.2.3. This is the cleanest and most idiomatic approach.

options.text: echo $CI_COMMIT_TAG | cut -c2-
options.explanation: This technically works, but it is non-idiomatic for shell. The standard approach is parameter expansion in bash.

question: Which type of git tag is recommended for releases and why?

options.text: Lightweight tag — it is created faster and takes less space
options.explanation: A lightweight tag is just a reference to a commit without metadata. For releases this is insufficient: no author, tag date, or message.

options.text: Signed tag — only GPG-signed tags are accepted in production
options.explanation: GPG-signed tags are an additional security layer, but not a mandatory requirement. Annotated tags are suitable for most teams.

options.text: Annotated tag — it contains author, date, message and is a full-fledged git object
options.explanation: Correct. An annotated tag is a full-fledged git object with metadata. It appears in git log, is supported by GitLab Releases, and works well with git describe.

options.text: Any tag type — it doesn't matter for CI/CD
options.explanation: Tag type matters: annotated tags contain metadata, appear as full-fledged objects in CI/CD systems, and are used in git describe.

question: What are Conventional Commits and why are they needed in the context of automated releases?

options.text: An IDE plugin that checks spelling in commits
options.explanation: Conventional Commits is a commit message format specification, not a spell-checking tool.

options.text: A standard required for GitLab CI to work
options.explanation: GitLab CI does not require Conventional Commits. It is a team convention that enables access to automated versioning.

options.text: A formatting standard that speeds up code review
options.explanation: Conventional Commits are primarily for machine parsing: tools like semantic-release and git-cliff read commits and determine the version type.

options.text: A commit format like 'type(scope): desc' that allows tools to automatically determine the version type and generate a changelog
options.explanation: Correct. feat: -> MINOR bump, fix: -> PATCH bump, feat!: -> MAJOR bump. Tools parse these prefixes and decide automatically whether a new release is needed and what kind.

question: What is the difference between a GitLab Release and a git tag?

options.text: GitLab Release is the same as a git tag, just with a different name in the UI
options.explanation: These are different entities. A git tag is a label on a commit. A GitLab Release is a page with description, changelog, artifact links, tied to a tag.

options.text: GitLab Release creates a tag automatically, git tag is manual
options.explanation: GitLab Release requires an existing tag. release-cli ties to a tag, but the tag must exist before the release is created.

options.text: You cannot create a git tag via CI, only GitLab Release
options.explanation: Git tags can be created from CI via git tag and git push. GitLab Release is created via release-cli.

options.text: Git tag is a label on a commit in the repository. GitLab Release is a page in GitLab with changelog, assets, and description, tied to a tag
options.explanation: Correct. A tag exists in git history. A Release is a UI layer on top of the tag: human-readable description, links to binaries, changelog for users.

question: You publish a Docker image with each release. Which tags should you apply to the image?

options.text: myapp:$CI_COMMIT_TAG — version tag (e.g., myapp:v1.2.3)
options.explanation: Correct. A version tag allows rolling back to an exact version: docker pull myapp:v1.2.3. Without it, reproducing a previous state is impossible.

options.text: myapp:$CI_COMMIT_SHA — commit SHA
options.explanation: A commit SHA for release images is redundant — a version tag already exists. SHA is useful for dev/staging images when debugging a specific commit.

options.text: myapp:latest — always points to the latest version
options.explanation: Correct. latest is a convenient alias for the latest stable release. New users get the current version without needing to know the number.

options.text: myapp:stable — a stable tag is needed for production
options.explanation: The stable tag is not a standard convention. latest typically implies a stable release. Adding non-standard tags without a clear need is not recommended.

question: A team uses semantic-release for automated releases. Which commit would trigger a MAJOR version creation (e.g., 1.x.x -> 2.0.0)?

options.text: major: remove deprecated API
options.explanation: The type major: is not defined in the Conventional Commits specification. semantic-release will not recognize this type.

options.text: feat!: remove deprecated method getUserById()
options.explanation: Correct. The exclamation mark after the type (feat!) indicates a breaking change. BREAKING CHANGE: in the commit body also works. semantic-release will bump MAJOR.

options.text: fix: remove deprecated method getUserById()
options.explanation: fix: without an exclamation mark will only trigger a PATCH bump. The commit type and the nature of the change must match: removing an API is a breaking change.

options.text: chore!: large refactoring of the codebase
options.explanation: chore! is technically a breaking change by format, but semantically chore is for auxiliary tasks without functional changes. semantic-release typically ignores chore for versioning.

question: When generating a changelog via git-cliff or conventional-changelog in a GitLab CI pipeline, the pipeline cannot see tag history. Why?

options.text: You need to install an additional gitlab-changelog plugin in the Runner
options.explanation: No such special plugin exists. The solution is to change the clone depth via the GIT_DEPTH variable.

options.text: Changelog tools don't support GitLab CI
options.explanation: Changelog tools work with git history, not the platform. The issue is not about compatibility.

options.text: Tags are not passed to CI — they must be created directly in the pipeline
options.explanation: Tags are passed to CI along with the repository. The only issue is clone depth.

options.text: By default GitLab CI does a shallow clone (GIT_DEPTH: 20), but changelog generation needs full history
options.explanation: Correct. A shallow clone contains only the last N commits without tags. For changelog generation, full history is needed: GIT_DEPTH: 0 or an explicit tag fetch.

question:
You are setting up a release pipeline. What is the problem with this configuration?

```yaml
publish:
  script:
    - npm publish
```

options.text: npm publish doesn't work in GitLab CI — you need to use yarn publish
options.explanation: npm publish works perfectly fine in GitLab CI. This is not the issue.

options.text: No version is specified for publishing — npm will take the version from package.json, which may not match the tag
options.explanation: Correct. The version in package.json must match the tag. If you don't update it via npm version ${CI_COMMIT_TAG#v}, the old version will be published.

options.text: npm publish will fail without NPM_TOKEN in the variables
options.explanation: True. Publishing to npm registry requires authentication via a token. Without NPM_TOKEN in CI variables, the command will return a 403 error.

options.text: The job will run on every commit to any branch, not just release tags
options.explanation: Correct. Without rules or only, the job runs on every push. Every commit to main would publish a new npm version, breaking versioning semantics.

options.text: All of the above options are incorrect
options.explanation: Some of the listed options are indeed correct.

question: How do you correctly link a GitLab Release to a CHANGELOG.md generated in a previous job?

options.text: Pass the content via the CI_RELEASE_DESCRIPTION variable
options.explanation: CI_RELEASE_DESCRIPTION is not a standard GitLab CI variable. No such mechanism exists.

options.text: GitLab automatically finds CHANGELOG.md in the repo root — no configuration needed
options.explanation: GitLab does not search for CHANGELOG.md automatically. You must explicitly specify description: './CHANGELOG.md' in the release block.

options.text: Specify the file path in the release:description field and obtain CHANGELOG.md via dependencies from the previous job
options.explanation: Correct. dependencies: [generate-changelog] loads the CHANGELOG.md artifact, and description: './CHANGELOG.md' passes its contents to GitLab Release.

options.text: Copy the contents of CHANGELOG.md directly into the description field via cat
options.explanation: Technically possible via script, but non-idiomatic. The correct approach is to pass the file path in the description field of the release block.

question: You notice that on every push to main, CI creates a new tag and publishes an npm package. Versions look like: 1.0.1, 1.0.2, 1.0.3... What is most likely configured?

options.text: A random configuration error — tags are creating themselves
options.explanation: Tags don't create themselves. This is explicitly configured behavior — most likely semantic-release or a similar tool.

options.text: semantic-release on the main branch with conventional commits analysis
options.explanation: Correct. semantic-release automatically creates tags on every merge to main. If commits are fix: type, it creates a PATCH release. This is standard trunk-based development behavior.

options.text: Developers manually create tags before each commit
options.explanation: If tags were created manually, they wouldn't be so regular and frequent.

options.text: GitLab automatically creates tags on merge into a protected branch
options.explanation: GitLab does not create tags automatically on merge. This must be explicitly configured in the pipeline.

question: What happens if you run 'git tag -a v1.2.3 -m "Release"' but don't run 'git push origin v1.2.3'?

options.text: The tag will be pushed to remote automatically via git hooks
options.explanation: Standard git hooks don't push tags automatically. A pre-push hook could do this, but that's a custom configuration.

options.text: The tag exists only locally, the CI/CD pipeline won't trigger, the release won't happen
options.explanation: Correct. A local tag is invisible to GitLab. CI/CD only reacts to events in the remote repository. Without git push origin v1.2.3, the tag remains only on the developer's machine.

options.text: GitLab will automatically pick up new tags on the next commit push
options.explanation: Tags are not pushed automatically along with commits. git push origin main will not send tags — an explicit tag push is needed.

options.text: GitLab will fetch the tag via fetch on the next MR open
options.explanation: GitLab doesn't fetch from a developer's local repository. The connection is one-way: the developer pushes to GitLab, not the other way around.

question: What is the role of the 'registry.gitlab.com/gitlab-org/release-cli:latest' image in a GitLab CI pipeline?

options.text: It is the default base image for all GitLab CI jobs
options.explanation: By default GitLab CI uses the ruby image, not release-cli. release-cli must be explicitly specified for release creation jobs.

options.text: The image automatically publishes all artifacts to npm and Docker Hub
options.explanation: release-cli only creates the GitLab Release page. Publishing to npm and Docker Hub are separate steps with separate tools.

options.text: This image is only for signing releases with GPG keys
options.explanation: release-cli does not handle GPG signing. Its purpose is to create GitLab Releases via the API with changelog, assets, and metadata.

options.text: The image contains the release-cli tool, which can create GitLab Releases via the API — enabling the 'release:' block in a job
options.explanation: Correct. release-cli is GitLab's official CLI tool for creating releases. Without this image (or manually installing release-cli), the release: block in a job won't work.
